t: The Franco-British counter-attack of September 1914 halted the German advance on Paris and ended the Schlieffen Plan, the German plan to defeat France in about six weeks.

A gap of 50 km opened between the German 1st and 2nd Armies, and the French 5th Army and the British Expeditionary Force advanced into it, while communications between the German armies and Moltke's headquarters were poor.

Casualty estimates differ widely: about 250,000 French, 12,733 British and 298,000 Germans in one estimate, and about 300,000 for all sides in another that questions whether the battle can be separated from its surroundings.
dyk: Joseph Gallieni commandeered about 600 Paris taxicabs on the night of 7 to 8 September to carry soldiers to the front; the meters ran, and the French treasury paid a fare of 70,012 francs.
ev: German armies win most of the battles of the opening campaign and overrun much of Belgium and northern France
Joffre abandons Plan XVII and the Great Retreat of the French and British begins
Moltke changes the German plan, and Kluck's 1st Army turns south-east and crosses the Marne
Joffre halts the retreat and orders a counter-offensive
The 6th Army meets the German IV Reserve Corps at the Ourcq, and the 5th Army and the BEF advance into the gap between the 1st and 2nd Armies
Hentsch's staff tour leads to a general German retreat to the Aisne
Moltke is replaced by Falkenhayn, and the First Battle of the Aisne begins
Both sides try to turn each other's northern flank in the Race to the Sea

f.date: 5 to 12 September 1914; the German retreat is also dated 9 to 13 September
f.place: Between Paris and Verdun along the Marne valley, northern France, on a west-to-east front of 230 km; the most severe fighting was in the western half
f.sides: France and the British Expeditionary Force under Joseph Joffre and John French, with 980,000 French and 100,000 British soldiers between Paris and Verdun on the eve of battle; Germany under Helmuth von Moltke, whose armies there numbered 750,000
f.outcome: The German 1st and 2nd Armies were at risk of encirclement and, with the other German armies, retreated to the Aisne, ending the German attempt to defeat France quickly; the armies then dug in on the Aisne.
